endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Assess and update risk measurement approaches at regular cadences.

endorsements.title: The PIEE Cycle: A Structured Framework for Red Teaming Large Language Models in Clinical Decision-Making
endorsements.quote: To operationalize this framework, healthcare institutions can begin by piloting the PIEE cycle in selected clinical departments where LLMs are already being applied or evaluated.

evidence.title: Toward Trustworthy Chatbots: A Protocol for Red Teaming for Health Related Conversations
evidence.effect: Protocol found 0/60 KA errors but 15% (12/80) BA errors, including 21% (4/19) high-severity.
evidence.quote: Our error framework identified that the primary safety risk was a failure to follow behavioral rules, rather than a lack of factual knowledge.

evidence.title: Testing the Black Box: Structural Barriers to Independent Evaluation of Consumer-Facing Health LLMs
evidence.outcome: Feasibility of independent context-specific evaluation of consumer health LLM risks
evidence.effect: Five linked barriers found, including terms-of-service and rate limits, non-resettable interfaces, and unsuitable accuracy criteria. No reliable independent evaluation framework exists.
evidence.quote: No reliable independent evaluation framework yet exists for examining how consumer-facing health LLMs behave in ordinary use.

commentary.bottom_line: One simulated study suggests that a structured red-teaming protocol can surface chatbot errors in a defined use context, finding errors in 12 of 80 BA probes and in 0 of 60 KA probes. No study shows that such protocols reduce patient harm in deployment, and a qualitative study reports barriers that may limit independent external evaluation.

perspectives.view: A single level 4 study tested the practice offline, using 160 probes rather than patients or clinical encounters. It measured whether the protocol detects errors and did not measure downstream outcomes. Indirectness, reliance on one study, and small counts such as 4 of 19 in the high-severity category support very low certainty.

The protocol found no errors in 60 KA probes and found errors in 12 of 80 (15%) BA probes. The study also reports 4 of 19 (21%) as high-severity, though the summary does not state what the 19 refers to. Error rates may differ by probe type. The study does not show whether detected failures were fixed before reaching users.

The qualitative study reported five linked barriers to independent context-specific testing of consumer health LLMs, including rate limits, interfaces that cannot be reset between probes, and unsuitable accuracy criteria. These barriers may reduce the fidelity and repeatability of red-teaming conducted outside a vendor's own environment.

NIST AI 600-1 calls for regular reassessment of risk measurement approaches but does not specify a protocol. The qualitative study found that terms of service can restrict independent testing and that no reliable independent evaluation framework exists. Contract terms that allow external evaluation may therefore be a precondition for carrying out this recommendation.

The tested protocol used 160 designed probes, including 20 multi-turn scenarios, for one chatbot. The study reports no staffing time or cost. Rate limits and non-resettable interfaces reported in the hazard study suggest that repeated testing at a regular cadence may require more effort than a single pilot in one department.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares organizations or deployments with and without a standardized context-specific risk measurement protocol on patient-level outcomes, error rates after deployment, or the rate at which detected errors are corrected. Studies are also needed on the staff time and cost of repeated red-teaming and on contract terms that permit independent evaluation.
commentary.underserved_note: Neither the testing study nor the hazard study reports probes or participants drawn from Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. A protocol checked only on probes of unstated language and literacy level may not detect errors that arise when those patients use the tool, so local protocols would likely need probes written for those groups.
